title: Conditionals, Hypothesis and Mood
orientation: Conditional grammar lets a writer distinguish an observed pattern, an open future possibility and an imagined alternative. Those distinctions matter in planning, policy analysis, advice and accounts of past decisions. A proposal might say what will happen if funding arrives, what would happen under an alternative budget, or what would have happened if earlier support had been available. These are different claims, not interchangeable tense exercises. Today you will first learn the familiar teaching patterns, then test their limits through mixed time reference, implied conditions, wishes, preferences and formal inversion. The final section distinguishes grammatical mood from the communicative purpose of a sentence. Review auxiliaries and modality before beginning. For cumulative revision, bring together clause structure, logical relationships and modal meaning from Days 13–17, and explain why your chosen form preserves the intended situation rather than simply matching a label.
outcomes: Distinguish open conditions from remote and counterfactual alternatives.
Construct common conditional patterns without treating them as exhaustive formulas.
Express wishes, preferences and regrets with appropriate time reference.
Use conditional inversion and mandative constructions with register awareness.
Explain how clause form, modal meaning and discourse context interact.

modules.title: Conditional meaning: patterns, reality and time
modules.definition: A conditional construction presents one situation as a condition under which another claim, action or conclusion applies. Its verb forms express both time relationships and the speaker’s way of presenting the possibility.
foundation: Start with the intended relationship. If you heat this wax, it melts describes a recurring result under the relevant conditions; this is often called the zero conditional. If the repair is finished tomorrow, we will reopen presents an open future condition, commonly called a first conditional. Present is normally used for future time in that conditional clause. If the repair were cheaper, we would proceed presents a more remote alternative. Past-form were here indicates distance from the actual situation, not a repair that happened yesterday.
intermediate: The second-conditional teaching pattern commonly combines a past form in the if-clause with would, could or might in the result. The third commonly combines past perfect with would/could/might have plus a participle: If we had kept a copy, we could have restored the file. It imagines a different earlier situation. Mixed patterns connect different times: If we had kept a copy, we would have the file now. The condition is earlier; the result concerns the present. Do not add perfect have mechanically to both clauses if the intended result is current.
advanced: These numbered categories are useful memory aids, not a complete grammar. Real past habits can use past forms in both clauses: If the roads flooded, we stayed home. Open conditions can contain a progressive, perfect or modal: If you have finished, send the form; If you can attend, call us. A condition may concern the appropriateness of a speech act: If you are hungry, there is soup in the kitchen offers useful information; hunger does not cause the soup to exist. Without your notes, I would have missed the detail expresses an implied condition without if.
expert: An open condition leaves its fulfilment unsettled in the discourse. A remote condition presents distance, often hypothetical or counterfactual, but remoteness is not a precise probability percentage. Context establishes whether an imagined alternative contradicts known facts. Will and would can occur legitimately in an if-clause when expressing willingness, insistence, politeness or a later consequence: If you will wait here, someone will help you. This differs from mechanically inserting future will in a neutral time condition. State the intended reading before judging a form; an assessment must supply enough context to distinguish a routine future condition from a modal exception.

patterns.meaning: A common open future pattern, with the result selected for meaning.

patterns.form: if + past perfect, would/could/might have + participle
if + past perfect, would + base + now
patterns.meaning: An earlier condition with a present hypothetical result.

examples.sentence: If the sensor detects smoke, the alarm sounds.
examples.analysis: The present forms describe a designed recurring relationship, not a universal scientific law.

examples.sentence: If we had booked a room, we would not be searching for one now.
examples.analysis: The past-perfect condition connects to a present result.

examples.sentence: If you will sign the register, I can issue a visitor’s pass.
examples.analysis: Will can solicit willingness; it is not an automatic error inside if.

contrasts.a: If the door is unlocked, I will enter.
contrasts.b: If the door were unlocked, I would enter.
contrasts.note: Both grammatical; the first leaves an open possibility, while the second presents a remote alternative in the stated context.

exceptions: A main clause can be imperative: If you notice damage, report it. A condition can be implied rather than introduced by if: With a stronger signal, we could communicate.

mistakes.problem: If the road were open now, we would have drive through it now.
mistakes.repair: If the road were open now, we would drive through it now.
mistakes.reason: For the intended present result, use would plus base drive; the original chain is malformed.

mistakes.problem: If I had saved it yesterday, I would have it now. [declared impossible because “mixed”]
mistakes.reason: The earlier saving condition and present possession result legitimately have different time reference.

glossary.definition: A conditional presenting fulfilment as unsettled rather than grammatically remote.
glossary.example: If she calls, I will answer.

glossary.definition: An imagined alternative contrary to an established fact.
glossary.example: If I had brought the key, we could have entered; I left it at home.

modules.title: Wishes, regrets, preferences and apparent situations
modules.definition: Wish and related constructions can express a desired difference from reality, a regret about an earlier event, a preference or an impression; each construction has its own complement pattern.
foundation: A present regret commonly uses wish plus a past form: I wish I knew the address means that I do not know it now. A past regret normally uses past perfect: I wish I had checked the address means that I did not check it, and now regret that omission. If only can express the same kind of wish with greater emphasis: If only we had checked. These forms locate an imagined difference from reality; past form after wish does not automatically locate the desired situation in past time. For an open desired future outcome, hope is normally appropriate: I hope the parcel arrives tomorrow.
intermediate: Wish has other patterns. I wish to speak to the manager is a formal expression of wanting; I wish you success expresses a good wish with two objects. Wish plus would often concerns a desired change in behaviour or circumstances: I wish the neighbours would lower the volume. It is not an unrestricted replacement for any state after wish. Would rather takes a base form with the same understood subject: I would rather wait. With a different subject, a past clause is common for a present or future preference: I would rather you waited outside. A past-perfect clause can express an earlier preference: I would rather you had told me yesterday.
advanced: It is time to leave is an ordinary infinitival expression. It is time we left also refers to the present or near future, despite the past form; it can imply that the action is overdue. As if and as though introduce an apparent or imagined comparison. He looks as if he is tired leaves tiredness plausible; He behaves as if he owned the office presents a distancing comparison. The construction does not always assert that its situation is false. Perfect reference is possible: She looks as if she has been running. Reduced forms also occur: She raised a hand as if to object.
expert: Irrealis were is available with be in remote comparisons and wishes, especially in formal prose: I wish I were there; she spoke as though she were the owner. Was is also established in many less formal standard contexts with first- or third-person singular subjects, so it should not be labelled universally ungrammatical. The deliberate choice of were can make the remote interpretation explicit. Subject identity matters in would-rather constructions; changing I would rather leave to I would rather you left changes whose action is preferred. Interpretation should therefore track the holder of the preference, the intended actor and the time of the preferred event separately.

patterns.meaning: Typically a desired difference in a present situation.
Typically regret about an earlier situation.

patterns.form: would rather + base / would rather + subject + past clause

examples.sentence: I wish I knew how to repair this lock.
examples.analysis: Knew expresses a current desired difference from not knowing.

examples.sentence: I would rather you had spoken to me before sending it.
examples.analysis: The speaker prefers a different earlier action by another person.

examples.sentence: The cyclist looks as though she has been riding in the rain.
examples.analysis: The comparison is consistent with an actual recent activity; it need not be false.

contrasts.b: I wish she were here now.
contrasts.note: Both grammatical; hope concerns an open desired outcome, while wish presents a desired difference from the current situation.

exceptions: Wish to means formally want to, not regret: We wish to renew the lease. As if can take a non-finite clause or a prepositional phrase: as if to protest; as though in pain.

mistakes.problem: I would rather to wait here.
mistakes.reason: Same-subject would rather selects a base form without to.

mistakes.problem: I wish I have checked it yesterday. [regret]
mistakes.repair: I wish I had checked it yesterday.
mistakes.reason: Past regret requires an appropriate earlier perfect form in this construction.

glossary.definition: Were used with a singular subject in a remote or contrary-to-fact construction.
glossary.example: If I were available, I would help.

glossary.definition: A choice of one situation over another.
glossary.example: I would rather walk than wait.

modules.title: Formal conditional inversion and conditional links
modules.definition: Conditional inversion places should, had or irrealis were before the subject in specified formal conditional patterns, normally replacing an if-clause without requiring a question meaning.
foundation: The common starting point is an if-clause: If you should need assistance, contact reception. In formal wording, omit if and place should before the subject: Should you need assistance, contact reception. This is a conditional statement with an imperative result, not an enquiry about whether assistance is needed. The form often presents a possible contingency politely or impersonally. It can be useful in notices and correspondence, but ordinary if is equally grammatical and often simpler. Inversion is therefore a resource for a particular register, not a compulsory sign of advanced writing.
intermediate: For an alternative past, Had I known the date, I would have attended corresponds to If I had known the date. Had is the auxiliary of the past perfect, and known remains a participle. For a remote present state, Were I free, I would join you corresponds to If I were free. Were followed by a subject and to-infinitive can present a remote future contingency: Were the supplier to withdraw, we would seek another. These patterns are limited: an ordinary lexical past verb cannot usually be moved in the same way. Wrote she earlier is not the normal conditional equivalent of If she wrote earlier.
advanced: Negative conditional inversion usually places not after the subject: Had we not checked the figures, the error would have survived. Contractions such as Hadn’t we checked can have other, interrogative uses and should not be substituted mechanically in formal conditional prose. Keep the result clause's modal and time reference unchanged when converting: Had she called, we might have helped retains possibility rather than certainty. A transformation from might have helped to would have helped strengthens the claim. The grammatical operation changes word order and removes if; it does not license extra factual commitments.
expert: Other conditional links have their own meanings. Unless commonly means except if: We will proceed unless the regulator objects sets an exception to proceeding. Only if states a necessary condition: We will proceed only if approval is granted does not itself promise that approval guarantees proceeding. Provided that, on condition that and as long as establish conditions or limits with register differences. In case often motivates a precaution rather than stating the condition under which an action will occur: Take a copy in case the network fails instructs taking it beforehand. Replacing all these links with if can alter the logical relationship. Analyse the condition's role before attempting an equivalent inversion or paraphrase.

patterns.meaning: Formal possible contingency, replacing if + subject + should.
Formal remote state or future contingency.

examples.sentence: Should the lights fail, use the marked exit.
examples.analysis: Should introduces a contingency; use supplies an imperative result.

examples.sentence: Had the clerk not kept a copy, we might have lost the record.
examples.analysis: Negation follows the subject, and might preserves a possible result.

examples.sentence: Were the lease to expire next month, the company would need alternative premises.
examples.analysis: Were to presents a remote future supposition.

contrasts.a: If you should require a receipt, ask at the desk.
contrasts.b: Should you require a receipt, ask at the desk.
contrasts.note: Both grammatical and close in meaning; the inverted version has a more formal register.

exceptions: Inversion applies to the licensed auxiliaries, not to every conditional verb. Retaining if as well as the inverted pattern is not the intended conversion: use If I had known or Had I known.

mistakes.problem: If had I known, I would have replied.
mistakes.repair: Had I known, I would have replied.
mistakes.reason: Remove if when forming this conditional inversion.

mistakes.problem: Had she knew, she would have objected.
mistakes.repair: Had she known, she would have objected.
mistakes.reason: Had selects the participle known, not past simple knew.

glossary.definition: A formal condition with auxiliary before subject and usually no if.
glossary.example: Had I seen it, I would have replied.

glossary.definition: A requirement without which a stated result cannot apply.
glossary.example: Entry is permitted only if a pass is shown.

modules.title: Mood, mandative meaning and cumulative analysis
modules.definition: Grammatical mood concerns conventional verb forms and clause patterns associated with statements, directives or non-actual situations; it is distinct from a speaker’s emotion and from the communicative function of a sentence.
foundation: Traditional teaching distinguishes indicative, imperative and subjunctive constructions. Most ordinary factual statements use indicative forms: The meeting starts at nine. An imperative typically uses a plain verb form with an understood addressee: Start at nine; do not enter. A sentence's grammatical form does not uniquely determine its social purpose. Can you wait? has interrogative form but usually functions as a request. Conversely an imperative can express an invitation or good wish rather than a harsh order: Have a seat; enjoy your visit. Analyse grammatical construction and practical purpose as separate questions.
intermediate: A mandative clause presents something as proposed, demanded or required. Formal examples include The policy requires that every visitor sign in and The adviser recommended that the hearing be postponed. Sign and be are plain forms, often called the mandative subjunctive. They do not acquire third-person -s or an ordinary tense ending in this pattern. British English also widely uses should: The adviser recommended that the hearing should be postponed. The plain form is especially characteristic of American formal usage but also standard in British English. These are established alternatives; changing should be to be is not a necessary correction.
advanced: The preceding verb does not automatically create mandative meaning. She insisted that she was innocent asserts a proposition; she insisted that the inspector be present demands a situation. Suggest can similarly indicate evidence, as in The marks suggest that the box was moved, rather than recommend an action. Formulaic subjunctives survive in expressions such as Long live the king and Be that as it may. Irrealis were is sometimes included under a broad traditional subjunctive label, while modern grammars may analyse it separately. The terminology varies; the form, meaning and distribution should remain clear.
expert: For cumulative analysis, ask five connected questions: what are the clause boundaries; what functions do the clauses perform; which time is intended; how strong is the modal claim; and does the wording fit the register? A conditional can contain an embedded content clause, a relative and a mandative requirement: If the policy that we adopted requires that each visitor sign in, the receptionist should explain the rule. Parsing those units prevents an agreement rule from being applied across an unrelated clause boundary. Use the phase assessment to revisit Days 13–18, and treat uncertain written responses as material for explicit self-review rather than an automatically awarded mastery score.

patterns.meaning: A standard mandative alternative, particularly familiar in British usage.

examples.sentence: The contract requires that the tenant pay on the first day.
examples.analysis: Pay is plain form in a mandative clause, despite singular tenant.

examples.sentence: The consultant recommended that the data should be checked independently.
examples.analysis: Should be is a legitimate British mandative construction.

examples.sentence: The witness insisted that she had seen the vehicle.
examples.analysis: Insisted introduces an asserted report here, so an indicative perfect clause is appropriate.

contrasts.a: They suggested that she be invited.
contrasts.b: They suggested that she should be invited.
contrasts.note: Both standard mandative alternatives; the second is particularly familiar in British English.

exceptions: A verb such as insist or suggest has more than one meaning and complement pattern. A that-clause after it is not automatically mandative. Modern descriptions may separate irrealis were from the plain-form subjunctive.

mistakes.problem: The rule requires that he signs in. [rewrite using the plain-form mandative]
mistakes.repair: The rule requires that he sign in.
mistakes.reason: The explicit transformation target selects the plain form; this does not declare every indicative mandative reading impossible.

mistakes.problem: They recommended that the gate should is locked.
mistakes.repair: They recommended that the gate should be locked.
mistakes.reason: The auxiliary after should must have base form be.

glossary.definition: Concerning a proposed, required or desired situation.
glossary.example: They demanded that the gate be opened.

glossary.definition: A clause construction typically headed by a plain verb and understood addressee.

questions.prompt: Which sentence presents an open future condition rather than a remote alternative?
options: If the printer worked now, we would use it.
If the printer had worked yesterday, we would have used it.
If the printer had worked yesterday, we would be finished now.
If the printer works tomorrow, we will use it.
questions.why: The present if-clause with tomorrow leaves a future possibility open; the other choices explicitly present remote alternatives.

questions.prompt: The key was not brought, and entry was impossible yesterday. Which sentence imagines that different past?
options: If we had brought the key, we could have entered.
If we bring the key, we entered.
If we had bringing the key, we could enter.
If we bring the key, we can enter.
questions.why: Had brought plus could have entered expresses the earlier counterfactual situation. If we bring the key, we can enter presents an open condition; the remaining alternatives have verb chains that do not express the stated past counterfactual.

questions.prompt: Choose the accurate analysis of “If she will wait, I can explain”. Here will means willingness.
options: Will legitimately expresses willingness in this if-clause.
Can must be replaced by will in every result clause.
Will is automatically wrong after if.
The sentence must refer to yesterday.
questions.why: Modal willingness is an established exception to the simplified future-clause rule.

questions.prompt: Express a regret about an omission yesterday: “I wish I ____ the serial number yesterday.”
options: have noted
noted now
had noted
would noting
questions.why: Had noted supplies the past-perfect form for an earlier regret.

questions.prompt: Which construction expresses a present preference about another person’s action?
options: I would rather you has wait outside.
I would rather you waited outside.
I would rather to you wait outside.
I would rather you to waiting outside.
questions.why: Would rather plus a different subject can take a past clause for a present or future preference.

questions.prompt: Complete the formal inversion: “Had I ____ the notice, I would have replied.”
options: saw
seeing
seen
see
questions.why: Auxiliary had takes the participle seen, not past simple saw.

questions.prompt: Which is the formal conditional counterpart of “If you should need a copy, contact reception”?
options: Should you need a copy, contact reception.
If should you need a copy, contact reception.
Need you should a copy, contact reception.
Should you needed a copy, contact reception.
questions.why: Should precedes the subject, if is omitted, and need remains a base form.

questions.prompt: A formal British report says “They recommended that the hearing should be postponed.” What is defensible?
options: Should must always be deleted as ungrammatical.
Recommended can never introduce a that-clause.
The hearing must take a plural verb.
Should be is a legitimate mandative alternative.
questions.why: British English accepts mandative should; the plain-form be alternative is also standard.

questions.prompt: Inspect the verb chain: “The policy requires that each visitor be registered.”
options: registered must become registering
No error
requires must become require
be must become is in every context
questions.why: Plain be is standard in a mandative clause; singular each visitor does not require is in that construction.

questions.prompt: In “She insisted that she was innocent”, the supplied context is an assertion, not a demand. Which analysis fits?
options: The content clause has no subject.
An indicative content clause reports her assertion.
Was must become be merely because insist occurs.
Insist must be followed by on here.
questions.why: Insist can report an emphatic assertion with an indicative that-clause; it does not always select on or a mandative.

questions.prompt: Label the time relationship: “If we had booked earlier, we would have a room now.”
questions.model: The condition concerns an unrealised earlier booking; the result is present hypothetical possession. It is a mixed-time conditional.
rubric: Identify past condition and present result separately.
Do not force perfect have into the current result.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Express an implied condition with if: “Without your map, we would have got lost.”
questions.model: If we had not had your map, we would have got lost.
rubric: Use an earlier condition appropriate to the past result.
Retain the map’s contribution without claiming a different route.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain “If the water freezes, the pipe bursts” versus “If the water freezes tonight, the pipe may burst”.
questions.model: The first presents a recurring conditional relationship in context; the second presents a possible event tonight and a possible result.
rubric: Identify general versus particular time reference.
Preserve may as possibility rather than certainty.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain why “If you are hungry, there is soup in the kitchen” need not claim that hunger causes soup.
questions.model: The condition makes the information relevant to the listener; it does not describe a causal creation of soup.
rubric: Distinguish relevance from causation.
Identify the practical offer of information.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Express a current wish: “I do not know her address. I wish I ____ it.”
rubric: Use past-form knew for a current desired difference.
Retain the stated lack of current knowledge.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Compare “I wish to renew the lease” and “I wish I had renewed the lease”.
questions.model: The first formally expresses wanting to renew; the second regrets a past non-renewal in the usual reading.
rubric: Identify the two complement patterns.
Distinguish future/intended action from earlier regret.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Does “She looks as if she is tired” necessarily say she is not tired? Explain.
questions.model: No. It presents an appearance consistent with tiredness; the situation may be true.
rubric: Reject automatic falsity.
Explain the appearance-based comparison.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Express a preference about another person: “I prefer you to tell me before leaving.” Use would rather.
questions.model: I would rather you told me before leaving.
rubric: Use the different-subject past-clause pattern.
Keep the intended actor as you.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Combine into an it’s time construction: “We need to leave now. We have delayed too long.”
questions.model: We have delayed too long, so it is time we left.
rubric: Use the conventional past-form clause.
Keep present urgency; do not report an actual past departure.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Order the formal condition: known / had / the date / we / , / we / would / have / attended
questions.model: Had we known the date, we would have attended.
rubric: Place had before we.
Use known as the participle and retain would have attended.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Remove if using conditional inversion: “If she were to withdraw, we might postpone the hearing.”
questions.model: Were she to withdraw, we might postpone the hearing.
rubric: Keep were to and subject order.
Preserve might rather than strengthen to would.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain why “We will enter only if invited” does not itself promise entry whenever an invitation comes.
questions.model: It makes invitation a necessary condition for entry, not a sufficient guarantee that entry occurs.
rubric: Identify the necessary condition.
Avoid reversing the conditional relationship.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Why is “Take a copy in case the network fails” different from “Take a copy if the network fails”?
questions.model: In case motivates taking a copy as a precaution beforehand; if normally makes taking it conditional on the failure.
rubric: Distinguish precaution from conditional timing.
Preserve the network-failure scenario.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Identify form and function: “Could you wait here, please?”
questions.model: Interrogative grammatical form; ordinarily a polite request in communicative function.
rubric: Keep form separate from function.
Do not label the whole clause imperative merely because it requests action.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Compare “The evidence suggests that the door was forced” and “They suggested that the door be repaired”.
questions.model: The first reports an evidential conclusion using an indicative past passive; the second recommends an action using a mandative plain form.
rubric: Identify evidence versus recommendation.
Explain the different complement forms.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Use the requested plain-form mandatives: “The rule requires that she ____ (be) present and that he ____ (sign) the register.”
rubric: Use plain forms in both subordinate clauses.
Retain she and he as the respective subjects.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: A policy note reads: “If the register were available now, we would check it. The adviser recommended that it should be copied. This is wrong because should can never follow recommend.” Revise only the false commentary.
questions.model: Replace the last sentence with: Mandative should is a standard alternative, particularly familiar in British English.
rubric: Retain the grammatical conditional and recommendation.
Correct the false universal claim rather than overcorrecting valid prose.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Parse the main relationships: “If the rule that we adopted requires that visitors sign in, the receptionist should explain it.”
questions.model: The outer if-clause supplies a condition. That we adopted is a relative modifying rule. That visitors sign in is a mandative content clause complement of requires. The main clause recommends an explanation.
rubric: Identify the relative and content clauses separately.
Keep the receptionist outside the subject of requires.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: If I had brought the receipt yesterday, I could have returned the item.
rubric: The past-perfect condition and modal-perfect result form a legitimate past counterfactual.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: If you will wait here, the receptionist can help you. [will expresses willingness]
rubric: Willingness licenses will in the if-clause.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: I would rather to stay.
rubric: Use a bare infinitive after same-subject would rather.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: I wish I had check the date.
corrections.model: I wish I had checked the date.
rubric: Past perfect requires the participle checked.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: If had we known the deadline, we would have replied.
corrections.model: Had we known the deadline, we would have replied.
rubric: Remove if in this inverted construction.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: Had she saw it, she would have objected.
corrections.model: Had she seen it, she would have objected.
rubric: Use the participle seen after had.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: They recommended that the gate should is repaired.
corrections.model: They recommended that the gate should be repaired.
rubric: Use base be after should.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the supplied context: The witness insisted that she was innocent. [an assertion]
rubric: An assertion after insisted can take an indicative that-clause.
Accept an equivalent repair preserving time, modal strength and intended meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

transformations.prompt: Use conditional inversion without strengthening the result: “If I had noticed the omission, I might have queried it.”
transformations.model: Had I noticed the omission, I might have queried it.
rubric: Omit if and invert had with I.
Keep might have queried and the earlier condition.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

transformations.prompt: Rewrite using a standard British mandative should construction: “The chair proposed that the vote be delayed.”
transformations.model: The chair proposed that the vote should be delayed.
rubric: Insert should before base be.
Keep the passive and the recommendation rather than turn it into an assertion.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

writing.prompt: Write a 100–140-word planning note for a small library. Include an open future condition, a remote alternative, a past regret and a mandative recommendation. Label each construction after your paragraph.
writing.model:
If the grant arrives next month, we will extend the evening opening hours for a short trial. If the building had a second entrance, we could separate deliveries from public access, but the present layout makes that difficult. I wish we had recorded delivery times last term; that information would help us judge the problem more precisely. The coordinator recommends that volunteers should sign in at the desk and record any access difficulties. These measures would improve our evidence without assuming that every delay has the same cause. Should visitors need assistance during the trial, the desk staff will explain the temporary arrangements and direct them to the accessible entrance.

Analysis: If the grant arrives is an open future condition; if the building had is a remote alternative; wish…had recorded expresses past regret; recommends…should sign is a British mandative pattern.
rubric: Include all four specified construction types with consistent time reference.
Keep recommendation distinct from a reported fact.
Use modals whose strength matches the planning context.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 13: identify the head of the subject noun phrase in “The absence of clear instructions could cause delays”.
recall.model: Absence is the head; of clear instructions is a dependent prepositional phrase.
rubric: Identify the full subject before analysing its head.
Do not use the nearer plural instructions as the main-clause subject.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 15: distinguish the that-clauses in “The rule that we revised requires that visitors sign in”.
recall.model: That we revised is a relative modifying rule; that visitors sign in is a content clause complement of requires.
rubric: Distinguish modification from complementation.
Identify the different functions rather than relying on that alone.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 17: explain the difference between “If she had called, we could have helped” and the version with would have helped.
recall.model: Could presents an available or possible outcome; would normally presents the result more definitely within the imagined alternative.
rubric: Preserve the modal difference.
Do not label the two results automatically identical.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

checklist: I identify the intended time of each conditional clause.
I recognise legitimate modal will inside an if-clause.
I preserve the actor and time in wishes and preferences.
I use conditional inversion without adding an extra if.
I accept standard British mandative should and distinguish recommendation from assertion.
